guide.title: Communication & Handoff
guide.lead: Good care is lost in bad handovers. Use a fixed structure on the radio and at the bedside, close the loop on every order, speak up clearly when something is wrong, and talk to the patient – at their level and in their language.

steps.title: Patient
steps.text: Age and sex – never the name.

steps.title: Problem
steps.text: Chief complaint and relevant history (risk factors, medicines).

steps.title: Findings
steps.text: Key assessment findings and vital signs.

steps.title: Treatment
steps.text: What you gave and how they responded.

steps.title: Ask
steps.text: Requests (orders, team activation), then confirm you were heard.

sections.title: Handover formats
rows: Age, Time of injury, Mechanism, Injuries, Signs (vital signs), Treatment
On arrival the team listens while one person speaks; then the transfer of the patient
notes: Add trends, response to treatment, scene details, pertinent negatives, and where belongings are.

sections.title: Talking to patients
rows: Get to eye level, use simple honest words, explain before you touch, keep the parent close
Introduce yourself, address them respectfully, check hearing aids and glasses, allow time
Face them in good light, write key questions, gesture; don't shout
Professional interpreter (phone or video); family only for basics
Calm voice, use their name, acknowledge feelings, offer choices

sections.title: Asking questions
items: Then closed to clarify: "Does it spread to your arm?"
Listen actively; repeat back what you heard

quiz.q: A radio report to hospital should NOT include:
options: The patient's full name and ID number

quiz.q: 'Give 0.3 mg epinephrine' – '0.3 mg epinephrine' – 'Correct.' This is:

options: "Can you tell me what happened before the pain?"
quiz.explanation: It can't be answered yes or no.

quiz.q: Best approach to a 7-year-old who fell off a bike:
options: Get to eye level, use simple words, explain what you're doing

quiz.q: Blood pressure is falling during transport. Using CUS, a team member says:
options: "I'm concerned about the falling pressure, I'm uncomfortable continuing without acting – this is a safety issue."
quiz.explanation: Clear words that can't be ignored.

options: Keep transmissions brief – typically under 30 seconds

quiz.q: 'History of COPD and heart failure; SpO₂ 88% on room air, 94% on 4 L/min by nasal cannula.' Which SBAR part is the history?
quiz.explanation: The oxygen findings and response belong to the assessment.

quiz.q: Best way to communicate with a severely hearing-impaired patient:
options: Face them, write key questions and use gestures
Speak normally and hope they lip-read
quiz.explanation: Use a qualified sign language interpreter if available.

quiz.q: The physician asks why you gave aspirin; you never mentioned hypertension, smoking or family history. Your report missed:
Communicating with command at a major incident:
options: Use incident command terms and send only essential information
Give a full report on every patient
quiz.explanation: Short, structured messages; METHANE for the first report.

quiz.q: '68-year-old, left-sided weakness from 2 hours ago, AF, stroke score 12, meets stroke alert – we need CT and the stroke team.' This covers:
quiz.explanation: AF is background; the request is the recommendation.

flashcards.question: Radio report contents
flashcards.answer: Unit and destination, age and sex (no name), chief complaint, relevant history, findings and vital signs, treatment and response, ETA, requests.

flashcards.question: SBAR
flashcards.answer: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation: a structure for handover.

flashcards.question: Closed-loop communication
flashcards.answer: Sender gives the order, receiver reads it back, sender confirms. Prevents errors in drugs and procedures.

flashcards.question: No names on the radio
flashcards.answer: Radio traffic can be overheard; protect confidentiality.

flashcards.question: Therapeutic communication
flashcards.answer: Active listening, open-ended questions, empathy without judgement, plain language.

flashcards.question: Language barriers
flashcards.answer: Use a professional interpreter (phone or video). Avoid family, especially children. Speak to the patient in short sentences.

flashcards.question: CUS words
flashcards.answer: Concerned, Uncomfortable, Safety issue: a clear signal that the team must stop and act.

flashcards.question: Beyond SBAR at handover
flashcards.answer: Trends and response to treatment, changes en route, scene details, pertinent negatives, family statements, belongings. Trauma: ATMIST.

critical.scenario: Chest pain patient: after nitroglycerin his BP drops from 128/78 to 82/50, HR 94 to 46; sweaty and confused, pulling at his mask. You're alone in the back.
critical.question: How do you handle communication?

options.t: Treat first, then give the hospital a brief update on the change and treatment (or ask your partner or dispatch to); use closed-loop with any orders

critical.explanation: A 20-second update lets the cath lab and team get ready.
critical.kpi: Prioritizes care and gives a concise update on deterioration

critical.scenario: 72-year-old with sudden confusion, mixing English and Mandarin, terrified: 'No hospital.' Her husband's English is limited. You need a stroke assessment.
critical.question: How do you manage the language barrier?

options.t: Use a phone or video interpreter service; meanwhile simple words, gestures and her husband for basics; continue the interpreter en route
Rely on the husband for everything

critical.explanation: Get last known well time from the husband.
critical.kpi: Uses professional interpretation to complete a time-critical assessment

critical.scenario: Rear-end crash: alert driver with a forehead bruise and midline neck tenderness refuses a collar and transport – she has to collect her children in an hour.
critical.question: How do you communicate for the best outcome?

options.t: Explain your specific concern (midline tenderness could mean a fracture), the real risk in plain words, offer to call the babysitter, and document a refusal with a witness if she still declines
Tell her she has no choice

options.f: She hasn't agreed to transport either.

critical.explanation: Concrete, caring explanations change more minds than threats.
critical.kpi: Uses therapeutic communication to address a refusal
